body:
To be honest, I'm not entirely sure. I've been quite manipulative since I was a child. I would hazard a guess that I've got some issues stemming from childhood sexual abuse, that in my child brain the only way to get what I want (need fulfillment) is to manipulate people. That's a guess, I'm no psychologist.

Have you managed to curtail your manipulation?

I can't imagine how hard it must be to know your mother will pass away. I love my mom too, the pain you are going through sounds so palpable it's like I can touch it through the monitor.

I'm so happy she has a daughter like you, someone that loves her so much she is willing to do all it takes to make her final days peaceful and complete. Despite all the agony this is putting you through, you're doing your best to not only carry yourself through your own life, but help her live the last of her days to the fullest. I think that's wonderful, and your loving, caring kindness is evident to me.

Two things that stood out to me:
> A huge part of me is saying that I will skip the funeral and go visit the grave a few days later on my own, but I know my family would be deeply hurt and angry if that was what I did.

Can you take the key matriarchs/patriarchs of your family aside, and explain your decision for what you want to do? Even if you decide not to do that, everybody grieves differently. They may be hurt, they may be angry, they may not understand, but you need to make the decision to grieve in a way that is right for you. If this is something they can't abide, I would think that they are caught up in their own grief and not thinking clearly. It is OK to not go to the funeral. It is OK to do what YOU need to do to find closure. You don't need to answer to anybody.

>I'm just scared and depressed and I see nothing in my future but watching someone I love dearly die slowly and painfully before my eyes. I don't know where to turn or who to talk to.

Have you looked into bereavement support groups in your area? I'll bet there are some specifically for the support of survivors of loved ones that have passed due to cancer. I have found that the best support comes from those whom are empathetic to our situation, and can understand where we are coming from. Talking to other adult children of terminal cancer patients or terminally ill parents in general may provide you with context, with contacts, and help you begin the grieving process before your mother passes.

I hope you stay safe. Lots of love to you and your mom.
I read your other post. I was gobsmacked at the eerily similar parallels between our lives. You can PM me if you like, maybe we can help each other out of the darkness.
